claim: In plants, transgenerational inheritance of certain epialleles has been observed.
source: In plants, transgenerational inheritance of certain epialleles has been observed but experimental evidence for selection of epigenetic variation independent of genetic variation is scarce.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Experimental evidence for selection of epigenetic variation independent of genetic variation is scarce.
source: In plants, transgenerational inheritance of certain epialleles has been observed but experimental evidence for selection of epigenetic variation independent of genetic variation is scarce.
evidence: This is a general assessment of the state of the field based on scientific knowledge.

claim: The experiment extended a previous selection experiment simulating selection in response to herbivory in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: We extended an experiment simulating selection in response to herbivory in Arabidopsis thaliana to assess a potential contribution of epigenetic variation to the selected phenotypes within three accessions.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: The experiment assessed a potential contribution of epigenetic variation to selected phenotypes within three accessions.
source: We extended an experiment simulating selection in response to herbivory in Arabidopsis thaliana to assess a potential contribution of epigenetic variation to the selected phenotypes within three accessions.
evidence: This describes the aim of the experimental design.

claim: Offspring from replicate populations and their ancestors were grown for two generations in a common environment to minimize maternal effects.
source: To minimize maternal effects, we grew offspring from replicate populations and their ancestors for two generations in a common environment and assessed the phenotypes in the second generation.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Phenotypes were assessed in the second generation.
source: To minimize maternal effects, we grew offspring from replicate populations and their ancestors for two generations in a common environment and assessed the phenotypes in the second generation.
evidence: This describes when phenotypic measurements were taken in the experiment.

claim: Weak evidence for the selection of epigenetic variation was found.
source: We found weak evidence for the selection of epigenetic variation: bolting time differed significantly in one accession.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Bolting time differed significantly in one accession.
source: We found weak evidence for the selection of epigenetic variation: bolting time differed significantly in one accession.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the phenotypic analysis.

claim: Significant differences between maternal lines suggested random residual or novel genetic and/or epigenetic variation.
source: Significant differences between maternal lines suggested random residual or novel genetic and/or epigenetic variation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences between maternal lines.

claim: The results are in conflict with a recent study reporting that environment-induced heritable variation is common in Arabidopsis.
source: Our results are in conflict with those of a recent study reporting that environment-induced heritable variation is common in Arabidopsis.
evidence: This compares the current findings to those of Lin et al., 2024.

claim: Reanalysis of data from Lin et al., 2024 showed that reported findings resulted from a mix-up of accessions.
source: Reanalyzing the data from that study showed that the reported findings resulted from a mix-up of accessions and, thus, reflected genetic rather than epigenetic variation between accessions.
evidence: This is based on reanalysis of RNA-seq data from the cited study.

claim: The findings from Lin et al., 2024 reflected genetic rather than epigenetic variation between accessions.
source: Reanalyzing the data from that study showed that the reported findings resulted from a mix-up of accessions and, thus, reflected genetic rather than epigenetic variation between accessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reanalysis of the Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: Unlike in animals, plant germlines are not set aside early in development but form later when somatic cells get committed to eventually form gametes.
source: Unlike in animals, plant germlines are not set aside early in development but form later, when somatic cells get committed to eventually form gametes (Schmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schmidt et al., 2015.

claim: Epigenetic marks affected by environmental conditions can potentially be inherited in plants.
source: As a result, epigenetic marks affected by environmental conditions can potentially be inherited.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that plant germlines form late in development.

claim: Epigenetic marks may contribute to adaptive responses in changing environments.
source: Therefore, epigenetic marks may contribute to adaptive responses in changing environments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential role of epigenetic marks.

claim: Spontaneous changes in DNA methylation occur much more frequently than genetic mutations.
source: Furthermore, spontaneous changes in DNA methylation, a mark associated with some naturally arising heritable epialleles in the plant model Arabidopsis thaliana (e.g., Soppe et al., 2000; He et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2018b), occur much more frequently than genetic mutations (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Johannes and Schmitz, 2019; Hazarika et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: DNA methylation is a mark associated with some naturally arising heritable epialleles in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Furthermore, spontaneous changes in DNA methylation, a mark associated with some naturally arising heritable epialleles in the plant model Arabidopsis thaliana (e.g., Soppe et al., 2000; He et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2018b), occur much more frequently than genetic mutations (van der Graaf et al., 2015; Johannes and Schmitz, 2019; Hazarika et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies on epialleles.

claim: The rates of epimutations might be sufficiently high to differentiate epigenetic from genetic variation, yet low enough to maintain a heritable response to selection.
source: This suggests that the rates of epimutations might be sufficiently high, differentiating epigenetic from genetic variation, yet low enough to maintain a heritable response to selection.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the frequency of epimutations.

claim: The potential role of epigenetic variation in adaptation depends on several factors: the rate of spontaneous epimutations, the influence of environmental effects on epigenetic variation, the heritability of epimutations, and the impact of epigenetic variation on the phenotype.
source: The potential role of epigenetic variation in adaptation depends on several factors: the rate of spontaneous epimutations, the influence of environmental effects on epigenetic variation, the heritability of epimutations, and the impact of epigenetic variation on the phenotype.
evidence: This is a general statement about factors affecting epigenetic adaptation based on scientific knowledge.

claim: To contribute to adaptation, epigenetic variation must be sufficiently stable and heritable over several generations so it can be subject to selection.
source: Importantly, to contribute to adaptation, epigenetic variation must be sufficiently stable, that is, heritable over several generations, so it can be subject to selection.
evidence: This is a logical requirement for epigenetic variation to play a role in adaptation.

claim: In non-model species, DNA methylation patterns assessed with reduced representation sequencing methods were frequently found to be associated with distinct environments or treatments.
source: In non-model species, DNA methylation patterns assessed with reduced representation sequencing methods were frequently found to be associated with distinct environments or treatments.
evidence: This is a general observation from the literature.

claim: Epigenetic variation was generally correlated with genetic variation in non-model species.
source: However, epigenetic variation was generally correlated with genetic variation (van Moorsel et al., 2019; Mounger et al., 2021; Boquete et al., 2022; Mounger et al., 2022; Ibañez et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in non-model species.

claim: High-resolution genome-wide studies in Arabidopsis have revealed extensive variation in DNA methylation patterns among different populations.
source: Likewise, high-resolution genome-wide studies in Arabidopsis have revealed extensive variation in DNA methylation patterns among different populations, but this variation was mostly associated with underlying genetic differences (Dubin et al., 2015; Kawakatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific Arabidopsis studies.

claim: DNA methylation variation in Arabidopsis was mostly associated with underlying genetic differences.
source: Likewise, high-resolution genome-wide studies in Arabidopsis have revealed extensive variation in DNA methylation patterns among different populations, but this variation was mostly associated with underlying genetic differences (Dubin et al., 2015; Kawakatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Studies on epigenetic recombinant inbred lines (epiRILs) suggest that epialleles can significantly contribute to phenotypic variation in plants.
source: Nonetheless, studies on epigenetic recombinant inbred lines (epiRILs) suggest that epialleles can significantly contribute to phenotypic variation in plants (Cortijo et al., 2014; Kooke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epiRIL studies.

claim: The role of spontaneous epigenetic variation in adaptation remains controversial.
source: Thus, while there are examples of pure epialleles Paszkowski and Grossniklaus, 2011 whose frequency is not related to genetic variation, the role of spontaneous epigenetic variation in adaptation remains controversial (Jablonka and Raz, 2009; Quadrana and Colot, 2016; Richards et al., 2017; Johannes and Schmitz, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations discussing the controversy.

claim: In most species, it is difficult to distinguish between epigenetic variation that results from genetic differences and pure epigenetic variation.
source: This is largely because, in most species, it is difficult to distinguish between epigenetic variation that results from genetic differences and pure epigenetic variation, which is independent of the genotype (Richards, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents a known challenge in the field.

claim: Disentangling genetic and epigenetic effects bears most promise in clonally reproducing species or in highly inbred species.
source: Disentangling genetic and epigenetic effects bears most promise in clonally reproducing species, such as dandelions or strawberries (Preite et al., 2018; Sammarco et al., 2024), or in highly inbred species, such as Arabidopsis.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a methodological consideration.

claim: In a previous experiment with Arabidopsis, selection was simulated in a rapidly changing environment.
source: In a previous experiment with Arabidopsis (Schmid et al., 2018b), we simulated selection in a rapidly changing environment.
evidence: This describes a previous study by the authors.

claim: Selected populations of two distinct genotypes exhibited significantly different flowering times and plant architectures when compared with their ancestral populations.
source: Selected populations of two distinct genotypes exhibited significantly different flowering times and plant architectures when compared with their ancestral populations, and these differences persisted for at least three generations in a common environment.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study cited.

claim: Phenotypic differences persisted for at least three generations in a common environment in the previous study.
source: Selected populations of two distinct genotypes exhibited significantly different flowering times and plant architectures when compared with their ancestral populations, and these differences persisted for at least three generations in a common environment.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study cited.

claim: A reduction in epigenetic diversity and changes in DNA methylation patterns were observed in the previous study, some of which were associated with phenotypic changes.
source: In parallel, we observed a reduction in both, epigenetic diversity and changes in DNA methylation patterns, some of which were associated with the observed phenotypic changes.
evidence: This is a finding from the previous study cited.

claim: The findings from the previous study indicated that epigenetic variation was subject to selection.
source: These findings indicated that epigenetic variation was subject to selection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of findings from the previous study.

claim: Most of the epigenetic variation in the RILs used in the previous study was likely retained as standing variation from the original hybridization event.
source: Therefore, most of the epigenetic variation in these RILs was likely retained as standing variation from the original hybridization event (Greaves et al., 2015) and did not accumulate during the selection experiment through spontaneously occurring or environmentally induced epimutations (Schmid et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The current study used Arabidopsis accessions from a previous selection experiment that investigated the effects of aphid herbivores on plant defensive traits.
source: Here, to assess the potential for epigenetic differentiation between selection treatments, we used a similar approach using Arabidopsis accessions from a previous selection experiment that investigated the effects of aphid herbivores on plant defensive traits (Züst et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the source of plant material for the current study.

claim: In the previous aphid selection experiment, mixtures of genetically uniform Arabidopsis accessions were grown for five generations in either insect-free cages or cages inoculated with different aphid species.
source: In this selection experiment, mixtures of genetically uniform Arabidopsis accessions were grown for five generations in either insect-free cages (control) or cages inoculated with different aphid species or a mixture of these species.
evidence: This describes the design of the previous aphid selection experiment.

claim: After five generations, genetic variation was significantly reduced, and populations were dominated by three accessions to various degrees.
source: After five generations, genetic variation was significantly reduced, and populations were dominated by three accessions to various degrees (Züst et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the previous aphid selection experiment.

claim: The three dominant accessions were Ma-0, Wei-0, and Wil-3.
source: After five generations, genetic variation was significantly reduced, and populations were dominated by three accessions to various degrees (Züst et al., 2012). To examine whether epigenetic variation was also selected within these three accessions (Ma-0, Wei-0, Wil-3), we compared phenotypic traits of selected populations
evidence: This identifies the specific accessions studied.

claim: Six independent replicate populations were used from each selection treatment after five generations of selection.
source: From each selection treatment, we used six independent replicate populations after five generations of selection and grew them together for two generations in a randomized planting pattern in a common environment.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Phenotypes were assessed only in the second generation to minimize confounding maternal effects.
source: To minimize confounding maternal effects, we assessed the phenotypes only in the second generation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: Genome-wide DNA methylation states were compared in a subset of mother plants used to set up the common-environment experiment.
source: We further compared genome-wide DNA methylation states in a subset of mother plants used to set up the common-environment experiment (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the methylation analysis performed.

claim: The experiment was designed to detect effect sizes of 10% or more at the significance level of p<0.05 with a statistical power of beta>0.80.
source: We designed the experiment to detect effect sizes of 10% or more at the significance level of p<0.05 with a statistical power of beta>0.80.
evidence: This describes the statistical power of the experimental design.

claim: Highly significant differences were found between accessions, replicate populations, and across five experimental blocks.
source: While we found highly significant differences between accessions, replicate populations, and across five experimental blocks (with plants generally growing worse in two blocks compared to the other three), we observed only few significant differences between selection regimes (control and the two different aphid treatments).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of phenotypic data.

claim: Plants generally grew worse in two blocks compared to the other three.
source: While we found highly significant differences between accessions, replicate populations, and across five experimental blocks (with plants generally growing worse in two blocks compared to the other three), we observed only few significant differences between selection regimes (control and the two different aphid treatments).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Only few significant differences were observed between selection regimes.
source: While we found highly significant differences between accessions, replicate populations, and across five experimental blocks (with plants generally growing worse in two blocks compared to the other three), we observed only few significant differences between selection regimes (control and the two different aphid treatments).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The differences between selection regimes were weak, with the percentage sum of squares explained by the contrasts being less than 1% and p-values ranging between 0.05 and 0.01.
source: These differences were weak, with the percentage sum of squares explained by the contrasts being less than 1% and p-values ranging between 0.05 and 0.01.
evidence: This quantifies the magnitude of differences between selection regimes.

claim: Minimal differences in DNA methylation patterns were found within accessions between plants from different selection regimes.
source: We found minimal differences in DNA methylation patterns within accessions between plants from different selection regimes, with 0.009% of all tested cytosines showing significant differences after correction for multiple testing (false discovery rate [FDR]<0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the DNA methylation analysis.

claim: 0.009% of all tested cytosines showed significant differences after correction for multiple testing (FDR<0.05).
source: We found minimal differences in DNA methylation patterns within accessions between plants from different selection regimes, with 0.009% of all tested cytosines showing significant differences after correction for multiple testing (false discovery rate [FDR]<0.05).
evidence: This quantifies the extent of differential methylation.

claim: There was no reduction in the amount of epigenetic variation in response to selection in the current study.
source: In contrast to our previous study (Schmid et al., 2018b), there was no reduction in the amount of epigenetic variation in response to selection.
evidence: This is a finding from the epigenetic variation analysis.

claim: Evidence for selection of epigenetic variation in this experiment is weak.
source: Thus, we conclude that the evidence for selection of epigenetic variation in this experiment is weak.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: A recent study claimed that environment-induced heritable variation is common in Arabidopsis.
source: In strong contrast to our findings, a recent study claimed that environment-induced heritable variation is common in Arabidopsis (Lin et al., 2024).
evidence: This refers to findings from another study.

claim: The aphid treatments in the current study had a strong impact on plant fitness and survival but not on epigenetic differentiation.
source: We were surprised about this finding because, in our experiment, the aphid treatments had a strong impact on plant fitness and survival but not on epigenetic differentiation.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: The design of the study by Lin et al., 2024 was susceptible to potential errors that confounded treatments with genetic variation at the beginning of the experiment.
source: We noticed that the design of the study by Lin et al., 2024 was elegant but susceptible to potential errors that confounded treatments with genetic variation at the beginning of the experiment.
evidence: This is an assessment of the Lin et al., 2024 study design.

claim: About 10% of the plants analyzed from Lin et al., 2024 belonged to accessions differing from the ones they had been assigned to.
source: Our analysis showed that about 10% of the plants that we could assess belonged to accessions differing from the ones they had been assigned to.
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: The error in Lin et al., 2024 stemmed from a mix-up of two selection treatments.
source: This error did not occur at random but stemmed from a mix-up of two selection treatments.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: The large effects assigned to environment-induced heritable variation in Lin et al., 2024 were very likely due to genetic differences between accessions.
source: Thus, the large effects assigned to environment-induced heritable variation were very likely due to genetic differences between accessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: Epialleles can be subject to selection and contribute to adaptation.
source: In summary, while epialleles can be subject to selection and contribute to adaptation (Schmid et al., 2018b), the frequency of these events remains unclear, and epigenetic differentiation in response to selection seems to require standing epigenetic variation within accessions.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The frequency of events where epialleles contribute to adaptation remains unclear.
source: In summary, while epialleles can be subject to selection and contribute to adaptation (Schmid et al., 2018b), the frequency of these events remains unclear, and epigenetic differentiation in response to selection seems to require standing epigenetic variation within accessions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge.

claim: Epigenetic differentiation in response to selection seems to require standing epigenetic variation within accessions.
source: In summary, while epialleles can be subject to selection and contribute to adaptation (Schmid et al., 2018b), the frequency of these events remains unclear, and epigenetic differentiation in response to selection seems to require standing epigenetic variation within accessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and previous work.

claim: Evidence for a role of environment-induced epigenetic changes in adaptation in Arabidopsis remains weak.
source: In contrast, evidence for a role of environment-induced epigenetic changes in adaptation in the model plant Arabidopsis remains weak.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024.

claim: The term 'block', especially the comparison between blocks 1–3 and blocks 4–5, was highly significant in all analyses.
source: The term 'block', especially the comparison between blocks 1–3 and blocks 4–5, was highly significant in all analyses and generally explained most of the total phenotypic variation (up to nearly 50% for leaf blade area, Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of phenotypic data.

claim: The block term generally explained most of the total phenotypic variation (up to nearly 50% for leaf blade area).
source: The term 'block', especially the comparison between blocks 1–3 and blocks 4–5, was highly significant in all analyses and generally explained most of the total phenotypic variation (up to nearly 50% for leaf blade area, Table 2).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of experimental blocks on phenotypic variation.

claim: For time to bolting, the term 'accession' explained most of the variation (23.2%).
source: The time to bolting was an exception because here the term 'accession' explained most of the variation (23.2%), followed by 'population' (8.8%), 'mother' (8.1%), and 'block' (6.5%).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of bolting time.

claim: The terms 'accession' and 'population' were consistently significant and explained a large fraction of phenotypic variation.
source: The terms 'accession' and 'population' were also consistently significant and explained a large fraction of phenotypic variation.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Effects of 'population' were likely due to differences in composition because accessions were not balanced between populations.
source: Effects of 'population' were likely due to differences in composition because accessions were not balanced between populations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the population effects.

claim: The interaction between 'accession' and 'population' was rarely significant and explained less than 1% of all variance.
source: Accordingly, the interaction between 'accession' and 'population', which would indicate differences between populations within accessions, was rarely significant and explained less than 1% of all variance.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The term 'mother' was occasionally significant, accounting for 5–10% of the total phenotypic variance.
source: Additionally, the term 'mother' was occasionally significant, accounting for 5–10% of the total phenotypic variance (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The selection treatment and its contrasts were rarely significant and explained less than 1% of the total phenotypic variation.
source: Compared with these previous terms indicating environmental and genetic influences, the selection treatment and its contrasts – as well as their interactions with the previous terms – were rarely significant and explained less than 1% of the total phenotypic variation (Tables 1 and 2, Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Significant differences in rosette diameter between the control and aphid treatments and between the two aphid treatments disappeared when accession Wil-3 was excluded from the analysis.
source: Furthermore, the significant differences in rosette diameter between the control and aphid treatments and between the two aphid treatments (Table 1) disappeared when we excluded the accession Wil-3 (with low replication at the level of maternal lines) from the analysis (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: The interaction between the two aphid treatments and the two accessions Ma-0 and Wei-0 remained significant when Wil-3 was excluded.
source: In this case, only the interaction between the two aphid treatments and the two accessions Ma-0 and Wei-0 remained significant (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis.

claim: Significant differences in bolting time were found between the control and the aphid treatments in Ma-0.
source: Separate analyses for each accession revealed significant differences in bolting time between the control and the aphid treatments in Ma-0 (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis shown in figures.

claim: A significant difference in trichome densities was observed between the two aphid treatments in accession Wei-0, but these were driven by some extreme values.
source: We also observed a significant difference in trichome densities between the two aphid treatments in accession Wei-0; however, these were driven by some extreme values (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis with a caveat about outliers.

claim: Several significant differences between selection treatments were found in accession Wil-3, but these should be treated with caution due to low replication at the level of maternal lines.
source: We found several significant differences between selection treatments in accession Wil-3 (Figures 2 and 3) but, again, considering the low level of replication at the level of maternal lines in this accession, these differences should be treated with caution.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis with a caveat about replication.

claim: The methylome of a subset of Wei-0 maternal lines from generation G6 (n=34) was investigated by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing.
source: We investigated the methylome of a subset of Wei-0 maternal lines from generation G6 (n=34), providing a more direct readout of the aphid treatment than would be obtained with plants from generation G7. We assessed the DNA methylation patterns of these plants by whole-genome bisulfite sequencing.
evidence: This describes the methylation analysis methodology.

claim: 3,573,936 cytosines were tested for differential methylation between ancestrals and the two aphid-selection treatments.
source: In total, we tested 3,573,936 cytosines for differential methylation between ancestrals and the two aphid-selection treatments.
evidence: This quantifies the scope of the methylation analysis.

claim: The number of significantly differentially methylated cytosines ranged from 101 to 131 across comparisons.
source: The number of significantly differentially methylated cytosines was similar in all comparisons: it ranged from 101, when the two aphid treatments were compared, to 131, when the L. erysimi treatment was compared with the ancestrals.
evidence: This quantifies the number of differentially methylated cytosines.

claim: About 0.009% of all tested cytosines showed significant differences, and they were dispersed across the entire genome.
source: Overall, about 0.009% of all tested cytosines showed significant differences, and they were dispersed across the entire genome (Figure 4a).
evidence: This quantifies and describes the distribution of differentially methylated cytosines.

claim: No evidence was found for a reduction or expansion of variation in DNA methylation between ancestrals and the two aphid-selection treatments in any of the three contexts of DNA methylation.
source: However, we did not find any evidence for a reduction nor an expansion of variation in DNA methylation between ancestrals and the two aphid-selection treatments in any of the three contexts of DNA methylation: CG, CHG (H being A, T, or C), and CHH (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from the epigenetic variation analysis.

claim: The majority of differentially methylated cytosines (DMCs) was in the CG context (87.6%).
source: The majority of DMCs was in the CG context (87.6%), and only a few were found in the CHG and CHH contexts (6.2% each).
evidence: This characterizes the sequence context of DMCs.

claim: About 13%, 15%, and 72% of all cytosines in the Arabidopsis genome are found in the CG, CHG, and CHH contexts, respectively.
source: Considering all cytosines of the Arabidopsis genome, about 13%, 15%, and 72% are found in the CG, CHG, and CHH contexts, respectively (Schmid et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a reference value from a previous study.

claim: There was a clear enrichment of DMCs in the CG context.
source: Thus, there was a clear enrichment of DMCs in the CG context, similar to our finding in the previous selection experiment (Schmid et al., 2018b) and consistent with the fact that methylation in the CG context shows the highest variability (Kartal et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the DMC analysis supported by citations.

claim: Almost all DMCs were located within or less than 2 kb away from genes (87.3%) or genes and transposable elements (98.1%).
source: Almost all DMCs were located within or less than 2 kb away from genes (87.3%) or genes and transposable elements (98.1%).
evidence: This characterizes the genomic location of DMCs.

claim: Most DMCs were related to differences in gene body methylation (gbM).
source: Together with the clear enrichment of the CG context, this suggests that most DMCs were related to differences in gene body methylation (gbM; Bewick and Schmitz, 2017, Muyle et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DMC characteristics supported by citations.

claim: There was an enrichment of several GO terms related to epigenetic regulation among genes with DMCs: 'histone methylation', 'DNA methylation', and 'chromatin silencing'.
source: There was an enrichment of several terms related to epigenetic regulation: 'histone methylation', 'DNA methylation', and 'chromatin silencing'.
evidence: This is a finding from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: GO terms associated with transport and growth in general were enriched among genes with DMCs, including 'positive regulation of cell proliferation', 'secondary cell wall biogenesis', and 'organic substance transport'.
source: The remaining terms could be associated with transport and growth in general, for example, 'positive regulation of cell proliferation', 'secondary cell wall biogenesis', and 'organic substance transport'.
evidence: This is a finding from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: The overall limited differentiation and the absence of reduced variation in DNA methylation suggest that there was only weak selection of specific DNA methylation sites.
source: However, the overall limited differentiation and the absence of reduced variation in DNA methylation suggest that there was only weak selection of specific DNA methylation sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the methylation analysis.

claim: RNA-seq data from Lin et al., 2024 was used to assess whether there was genetic variation associated with treatments.
source: To assess whether there was any genetic variation associated with the treatments in the experiment described by Lin et al., 2024, we used their RNA-seq data (PRJNA997595) on a subset of 190 plants that supposedly included four accessions.
evidence: This describes the reanalysis methodology.

claim: Pairwise genetic distances were compared and accessions most closely related to the experimental plants were identified using 10,000 randomly drawn genes.
source: We compared pairwise genetic distances and identified the accessions most closely related to the experimental plants. We used 10,000 randomly drawn genes for the analyses and were left with up to 13,418 variants after filtering for coverage between 10 and 1000 in at least four plants per treatment and accession.
evidence: This describes the reanalysis methodology.

claim: Two presumed accessions, Abd-0 and TRE-1, were each represented by two genetically distinct clusters.
source: Visualizing pairwise genetic distances between all plants revealed that two presumed accessions, Abd-0 and TRE-1, were each represented by two genetically distinct clusters (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: The genetically distinct groups in Lin et al., 2024 had been associated with different selection treatments, leading to confounding of selection treatments with accessions.
source: When we visualized each accession separately, highlighting the treatments, we found that the genetically distinct groups had been associated with different selection treatments, leading to an unwanted confounding of selection treatments with accessions.
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: In the high Cd treatment, the plants labeled as Abd-0 were in fact from another accession (Ws-2).
source: Specifically, in the high Cd treatment, the plants labeled as Abd-0 were in fact from another accession, and the same happened in the drought treatment where plants labeled as TRE-1 came from another accession (Figure 5b). When we compared the genomes of these experimental plants to those of publicly available accessions, we found that the genetically distinct plants from the high Cd treatment belonged to the accession Ws-2
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis comparing to public data.

claim: In the drought treatment, plants labeled as TRE-1 came from another accession (Fei-0).
source: Specifically, in the high Cd treatment, the plants labeled as Abd-0 were in fact from another accession, and the same happened in the drought treatment where plants labeled as TRE-1 came from another accession (Figure 5b). When we compared the genomes of these experimental plants to those of publicly available accessions, we found that the genetically distinct plants from the high Cd treatment belonged to the accession Ws-2 and those from the drought treatment belonged to the accession Fei-0, both accessions that were otherwise included in the experiment (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis comparing to public data.

claim: When experimental plants were assigned to publicly available accessions, the distances to the closest accessions were between 0.0003 and 0.0034 (0.0019 on average).
source: Notably, when we assigned the experimental plants to publicly available accessions, the distances to the closest accessions were between 0.0003 and 0.0034 (0.0019 on average), compared with distances to accessions Abd-0 and TRE-1, respectively, ranging from 0.358 to 0.451 (0.414 on average).
evidence: This quantifies the genetic similarity to correct accessions.

claim: Distances to accessions Abd-0 and TRE-1 ranged from 0.358 to 0.451 (0.414 on average).
source: Notably, when we assigned the experimental plants to publicly available accessions, the distances to the closest accessions were between 0.0003 and 0.0034 (0.0019 on average), compared with distances to accessions Abd-0 and TRE-1, respectively, ranging from 0.358 to 0.451 (0.414 on average).
evidence: This quantifies the genetic distance to originally assigned accessions.

claim: With the original accession labels from Lin et al., 2024, large distances were found in all three classes (within lineage, within accessions, and between accessions).
source: These expectations were not met with the original accession labels; instead, we found large distances in all three classes.
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of genetic distances.

claim: With the re-assigned accession labels (Ws-2 for Abd-0 in high Cd treatment and Fei-0 for TRE-1 in drought treatment), distances were close to zero within lineages and within accessions, and large between accessions.
source: In contrast, the same evaluation with the re-assigned accession labels Ws-2 (for Abd-0 in high Cd treatment) and Fei-0 (for TRE-1 in drought treatment) confirmed the expectations of close to zero distances in classes (i) and (ii), and large distances in class (iii).
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis with corrected labels.

claim: 20 out of 190 plants (~10.5%) were reassigned to new accessions in the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024.
source: In summary, our analysis reassigned 20 out of 190 plants (~10.5%) to new accessions.
evidence: This quantifies the extent of the accession mix-up.

claim: The misassignment in Lin et al., 2024 explains the large effects interpreted as environment-induced heritable variation, which are really effects of genetic differences between accessions.
source: This misassignment explains the large effects interpreted as environment-induced heritable variation by Lin et al., 2024 that, as we show here, are really effects of genetic differences between accessions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the reanalysis.

claim: Flowering time in Arabidopsis has a strong genetic component.
source: This finding is in line with the notion that flowering time in Arabidopsis has a strong genetic component (Atwell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: There are three possible explanations for maternal line effects in genetically uniform accessions: maternal effects, initial genetic or epigenetic differences between maternal lines, and/or differential gain of genetic or epigenetic variation between maternal lines during the experiment.
source: In genetically uniform accessions, there are three possible explanations for these maternal line effects: (i) maternal effects, (ii) initial genetic or epigenetic differences between maternal lines that resulted in founder effects, and/or (iii) a differential (but selection treatment-independent) gain of genetic or epigenetic variation between maternal lines during the five generations of the selection experiment.
evidence: This is a logical enumeration of possible explanations.

claim: Seeds of single accessions obtained from NASC may not have been derived from homozygous, genetically uniform plants.
source: First, seeds of single accessions obtained from NASC may not have been derived from homozygous, genetically uniform plants.
evidence: This is a potential source of genetic variation in the material.

claim: Genotyping errors could occur during the identification of plants representing the accessions of interest.
source: Second, there could have been genotyping errors occurring during the identification of plants representing the accessions of interest.
evidence: This is a potential source of error in experiments.

claim: Plants of the two accessions showing no effect in Lin et al., 2024 (Ang-0 and Tol-0) were genetically very similar to each other and were found identical to their accessions using publicly available data.
source: Plants of the two accessions showing no effect were genetically very similar to each other and were found identical to their accessions using publicly available data from over 1000 accessions (1001genomes.org).
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: Plants from the presumed accessions with strong effects in Lin et al., 2024 (Abd-0 and TRE-1) showed strong genetic differences between treatments.
source: However, plants from the presumed accessions with strong effects, Abd-0 and TRE-1, showed strong genetic differences between treatments, which results from a mix-up of accessions while preparing or conducting the experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from the reanalysis of Lin et al., 2024 data.

claim: Residual genetic variation and newly acquired (epi)genetic variation could be experimentally distinguished in certain setups.
source: While experimental errors can only be addressed by verifying the material's identity at each step (which can be costly and challenging), residual genetic variation and newly acquired (epi)genetic variation could be experimentally distinguished in certain setups.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration.

claim: If phenotypic differences between replicate populations of single accessions already occurred before imposing the selection treatments, it would suggest that the populations were (epi)genetically distinct from each other.
source: If phenotypic differences between replicate populations of single accessions already occurred before imposing the selection treatments, it would suggest that the populations were (epi)genetically distinct from each other.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental interpretation.

claim: If phenotypic differences between replicate populations emerge after the treatment and are maintained in a common environment, then this indicates that variation was gained during the treatment.
source: However, if phenotypic differences between replicate populations emerge after the treatment and are maintained in a common environment, then this indicates that variation was gained during the treatment.
evidence: This is a logical inference about experimental interpretation.

claim: Differences between replicate populations due to founder effects or drift may be as relevant regarding evolutionary processes as are consistent differences between selection treatments.
source: We note that differences between replicate populations due to founder effects or drift may be as relevant regarding evolutionary processes as are consistent differences between selection treatments (Crow and Kimura, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to evolutionary theory.

claim: In the previous study using RILs, epialleles differing between selected and ancestral plants persisted for multiple generations in a state that did not match the underlying genotype but finally converged to it.
source: We hypothesized that the epialleles differing between selected and ancestral plants persisted for multiple generations in a state that did not match the underlying genotype but finally converged to it (Schmid et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the previous study.

claim: This scenario of epiallele convergence was impossible in the present study because distinct accessions were used.
source: This scenario was impossible in the present study because we used distinct accessions.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the difference between studies.

claim: Residual heterozygosity in one of the RILs might have contributed to observations in the previous study.
source: In our previous study (Schmid et al., 2018b), we also noted some residual heterozygosity in one of the RILs, which might have contributed to our observations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the previous study.

claim: Studies on a wide range of plant species that included genetically non-uniform populations consistently reported a significant correlation between genetic and epigenetic variation.
source: Studies on a wide range of plant species that included genetically non-uniform populations consistently reported a significant correlation between genetic and epigenetic variation (van Moorsel et al., 2019; Mounger et al., 2021; Boquete et al., 2022; Mounger et al., 2022; Ibañez et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in various species.

claim: There are very few studies in natural systems that demonstrate genetically independent, heritable epigenetic variation in the absence of environmental triggers or after accounting for maternal effects.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there are very few studies in natural systems that demonstrate genetically independent, heritable – that is, 'true' epigenetic – variation in the absence of environmental triggers or after accounting for maternal effects.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field.

claim: Maternal effects may explain the differences in flowering time between genetically identical apomictic dandelions collected in the field.
source: For example, maternal effects may explain the differences in flowering time between genetically identical apomictic dandelions collected in the field (Wilschut et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a dandelion study.

claim: An epigenetic memory effect of heat treatments with changes in DNA methylation in the CHG context has been shown in the clonally reproducing duckweed Lemna minor.
source: One example of inheritance of true epigenetic variation has recently been shown in the clonally reproducing duckweed Lemna minor (van Antro et al., 2023). The authors report an epigenetic memory effect of heat treatments with changes in DNA methylation in the CHG context.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a duckweed study.

claim: The epigenetic memory effect in duckweed might be due to differences in mitotic vs. meiotic inheritance.
source: However, this might be due to differences in mitotic (i.e., clonal) vs. meiotic inheritance.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Certain epigenetic states are faithfully inherited during mitosis.
source: While it has long been known that certain epigenetic states are faithfully inherited during mitosis (Meins, 1983; Meins, 1986), recent evidence shows that meiosis is accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming in plants (Slotkin et al., 2009; She and Baroux, 2014; She and Baroux, 2015; Park et al., 2016; Schmid et al., 2018a; Borg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mitotic inheritance.

claim: Meiosis is accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming in plants.
source: While it has long been known that certain epigenetic states are faithfully inherited during mitosis (Meins, 1983; Meins, 1986), recent evidence shows that meiosis is accompanied by epigenetic reprogramming in plants (Slotkin et al., 2009; She and Baroux, 2014; She and Baroux, 2015; Park et al., 2016; Schmid et al., 2018a; Borg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to recent studies.

claim: It may be interesting to study epigenetic inheritance in species that generally reproduce clonally through mitosis but distinguish between vegetative reproduction through multicellular meristems and apomictic reproduction through an unreduced, unrecombined egg cell.
source: Thus, it may be interesting to study epigenetic inheritance in species that generally reproduce clonally through mitosis but distinguish between vegetative reproduction through multicellular meristems and apomictic reproduction through an unreduced, unrecombined egg cell (Schmid, 1990; Koltunow and Grossniklaus, 2003; Schmidt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research supported by citations.

claim: The selection experiment began with a collection of 27 Arabidopsis accessions.
source: In brief, the experiment began with a collection of 27 Arabidopsis accessions.
evidence: This describes the starting material of the original selection experiment.

claim: Seeds obtained from NASC were expected to represent genetically uniform accessions and were propagated for one generation.
source: Seeds obtained from NASC were expected to represent genetically uniform accessions and were propagated for one generation.
evidence: This describes the preparation of material for the original selection experiment.

claim: Experimental populations with 20 seeds from each accession were planted in cages for the selection treatment.
source: For the selection treatment, experimental populations with 20 seeds from each accession were planted in cages.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup of the original selection experiment.

claim: Different aphid species or a mixture were released into the cages 17 days after sowing.
source: 17 days after sowing, different aphid species or a mixture were released into the cages (none as a control).
evidence: This describes the treatment application in the original selection experiment.

claim: After 60 days, all plants in a cage were harvested and a population of 800 seeds was sown representing the next generation.
source: After 60 days, all plants in a cage were harvested and a population of 800 seeds was sown representing the next generation.
evidence: This describes the generational cycling in the original selection experiment.

claim: Each population was maintained over five generations of selection, with six replicate populations per selection treatment.
source: Each population was maintained over five generations of selection, with six replicate populations per selection treatment.
evidence: This describes the replication structure of the original selection experiment.

claim: At the end of the selection experiment, the genetic composition of the populations was assessed.
source: At the end of the selection experiment, the genetic composition of the populations was assessed (Züst et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the final assessment of the original selection experiment.

claim: Ma-0 and Wei-0 were chosen because they were the most frequent after the aphid selection treatments.
source: The accessions Ma-0 and Wei-0 were chosen because they were the most frequent after the aphid selection treatments.
evidence: This explains the rationale for accession selection.

claim: Wil-3 was chosen because it is a trichome-less accession that persisted across all treatments.
source: Wil-3 was chosen because it is a trichome-less accession that persisted across all treatments.
evidence: This explains the rationale for including Wil-3.

claim: The study focused on three selection treatments: the two single-aphid treatments with Bravicoryne brassicae (BB) and Liphaphis erysimi (LE), and the control without aphid treatment.
source: We further focused on three selection treatments: the two single-aphid treatments with Bravicoryne brassicae (BB) and Liphaphis erysimi (LE), and the control without aphid treatment.
evidence: This describes the treatments included in the current study.

claim: Offspring from the plants that were used to set up the original selection experiment were included as 'ancestrals'.
source: Additionally, we included offspring from the plants that were used to set up the original selection experiment, here referred to as 'ancestrals'.
evidence: This describes the inclusion of ancestral controls.

claim: All selected plants were grown together for one generation to minimize confounding maternal effects.
source: All selected plants were grown together for one generation to minimize confounding maternal effects.
evidence: This describes the experimental design to control for maternal effects.

claim: For each treatment and accession, five mother plants from each of the six populations per selection treatment were planned to be used.
source: For each treatment and accession, we planned to use five mother plants from each of the six populations per selection treatment.
evidence: This describes the planned experimental design.

claim: Due to the rarity of some accessions in certain populations, mothers from other populations of the same selection treatment were used to fill up missing plants.
source: However, due to the rarity of some accessions in certain populations, we supplemented with mothers from other populations of the same selection treatment to fill up missing plants (360 maternal seed families were planned but ultimately only 261 were used).
evidence: This describes a deviation from the planned design.

claim: Population identity and maternal plant identity were used as random terms in the analysis.
source: We accounted for this in our analysis by using population identity (n=6 replicates × 3 selection treatments + ancestrals = 19) and maternal plant identity (n=261 < 5 mothers × 3 accessions × 18 populations for control and selection-treatment plants + 30 mothers × 3 accessions for ancestrals = 360) as random terms.
evidence: This describes the statistical model structure.

claim: Between 5 and 150 offspring of each mother were grown and phenotyped in the second generation (n=1,800).
source: After the first generation of the present experiment (the sixth generation [G6] in reference to the selection experiment), between 5 (planned) and 150 (if there was only a single mother available) offspring of each mother were grown and phenotyped in the second (G7) generation (n=1,800).
evidence: This describes the number of offspring phenotyped.

claim: Both generations were grown in a common environment in a fully randomized block design.
source: Both generations were grown in a common environment in a fully randomized block design.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: If there were differences between selection treatments, they would have been maintained for two generations in the absence of selection by aphids.
source: Hence, if there were differences between selection treatments, they would have been maintained for two generations in the absence of selection by aphids.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what the experimental design would reveal.
